title: Learning to read your crochet
subtitle: How to see what the stitches are telling you without counting constantly
excerpt: Reading your crochet means being able to look at the fabric and understand what has happened — where you are in the pattern, whether a stitch looks right, whether you have increased or decreased correctly. It takes time to develop and comes from handling the work deliberately.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet — developing crochet instinct. Standard crochet foundation teaching.

glossaryTerms.definition: The structural parts of a crochet stitch: the V-shaped top loops, the post (vertical body), and the base bar at the foundation. Being able to identify these parts by sight in the fabric is the start of reading crochet.
The ability to look at crochet fabric and understand its structure without reference to the written pattern — recognising stitch types, seeing increases and decreases, finding where the round starts.

heroPrompt: Close-up of a crochet swatch in cream DK cotton with a finger pointing to a single stitch top, showing the V-shape clearly against the surrounding fabric texture.

content.text: An experienced crocheter looks at the fabric and knows where they are in the pattern, whether a stitch was worked correctly, and where a mistake is. This is
— and it is learned by looking carefully at the fabric while working, not by working faster.
Every stitch has the same basic

: two loops at the top forming a V, a post going down, and a base bar connecting it to the row below. After working a row of double crochet, stop and study the V-shapes. Touch each one. Count them. Turn the work over and look at the wrong side. The stitch structure looks different from each angle — knowing both views helps you recognise a stitch from any direction.
After completing a row, put the hook down and look at the fabric before turning. Identify the first stitch and the last stitch. Find the turning chain. Count the stitches by sight.

In a round piece, look at where the round started and identify the stitch marker position. Try to find the marker without looking at where you placed it — can you see the change in height at the round join?

When something looks wrong — a slight bump, an uneven row, a stitch that looks different from its neighbours — stop and investigate. Touch the suspect stitch. Find the post, find the base bar. What is different about it?
Picking up a project after weeks away and knowing exactly where you are without notes.
Spotting a miscounted stitch three rows back before it becomes a wider problem.
Knowing whether a stitch pattern is correct without checking the written row every 2 stitches.
